items.title: October security update switches NTLMv1-derived SSO credentials from audit to block on devices without Credential Guard
items.officialTitle: Take action: NTLMv1 hardening changes might affect network connections on devices without Credential Guard
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft writes: “Beginning with the October 2026 security update … Windows uses Enforce mode as the internal default behavior instead of Audit mode, if the registry key BlockNtlmv1SSO has not been previously configured.” The October update shipped on 13 October 2026, so no future date governs it.
items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.fingerprint: From the October 2026 security update, Windows 11 24H2, 25H2 and 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 block the generation of NTLMv1-derived credentials for single sign-on by default when Credential Guard is disabled and the BlockNtlmv1SSO registry value has not been set. Wi-Fi, Ethernet and VPN connections that use MS-CHAPv2 (PEAP-MSCHAPv2, EAP-MSCHAPv2) for SSO may stop connecting automatically; manual credentials still work but cannot be saved. Setting BlockNtlmv1SSO to 0 returns a device to audit mode (Event ID 4024 in Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational); value 1 enforces and logs Event ID 4025. Microsoft recommends moving to EAP-TLS or PEAP-TLS.
items.why: A wave of Wi-Fi or VPN failures after Patch Tuesday will look like an outage or a credential attack. The temporary fix, BlockNtlmv1SSO = 0, re-enables a weak credential path; anyone who sets it fleet-wide without an expiry undoes the hardening.
items.action: Inventory 802.1X and VPN profiles that still use PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-MSCHAPv2 on Windows 11 24H2+ and Server 2025 without Credential Guard; plan the move to EAP-TLS; if you must return devices to audit mode, scope it by group, record an end date and watch Event ID 4024 until it stops.

items.title: Microsoft adds 30 Office CVEs it left out of October Patch Tuesday, three of them Critical, and ships the Office for Mac fixes
items.officialTitle: October 2026 Security Updates — revision of 15 October 2026
items.publishedSource: MSRC CVRF API document 2026-Oct, current release 15 October 2026 07:00 UTC, read 16 October 2026
items.fingerprint: Microsoft revised its October 2026 security update document on 15 October 2026. It added 30 Office CVEs with the note 'This CVE was addressed by updates that were released in October 2026, but the CVE was inadvertently omitted from the October 2026 Security Updates'; three are Critical — Word remote code execution CVE-2026-108439 (CVSS 8.8) and CVE-2026-108440, and Outlook remote code execution CVE-2026-108448 (7.5). The same revision announced the Office for Mac security updates for 92 October CVEs. Customers who already installed the October updates need no further action.
items.why: Vulnerability scanners and patch dashboards keyed on the 13 October CVE list did not know these 30 CVEs; a Critical Word or Outlook RCE that a report shows as absent is one nobody verifies. Macs with Office need their own update.
items.action: Refresh your scanner's CVE feed and confirm Defender Vulnerability Management shows CVE-2026-108439, -108440 and -108448 as remediated on Windows Office builds from October; push the Office for Mac October update through your Mac management channel.

items.title: Two identity-library CVEs published on 15 October: Microsoft Identity Web elevation of privilege and MSAL for Node.js information disclosure
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Identity Web Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability; Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) for Node.js Information Disclosure Vulnerability
items.publishedSource: MSRC CVRF API document 2026-Oct, both CVEs 'Information published' 15 October 2026, read 16 October 2026
items.fingerprint: CVE-2026-80092: 'Authentication bypass by assumed-immutable data in Microsoft Identity Web allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network' — Important, CVSS 5.3, Exploited: No, Publicly disclosed: No. CVE-2026-109461: 'Origin validation error in Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) for Node.js allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network' — Important, CVSS 5.9, Exploited: No. Revised 19 October 2026: the Security Updates table now lists Microsoft Identity Web v3 and v4 separately with their affected version ranges; the fixed versions are 3.16.0 and 4.16.1 (MSRC calls it an informational change).
items.why: These are libraries inside your own line-of-business apps, so no Windows or Office patch covers them; an app that authorizes on a claim the attacker can influence is an access-control flaw in software you own.
items.action: Ask application owners which web APIs use Microsoft.Identity.Web and which Node.js services use @azure/msal-node; a v3 app needs 3.16.0 and a v4 app 4.16.1, per the revised MSRC table.
items.fingerprintBefore: CVE-2026-80092: 'Authentication bypass by assumed-immutable data in Microsoft Identity Web allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network' — Important, CVSS 5.3, Exploited: No, Publicly disclosed: No. CVE-2026-109461: 'Origin validation error in Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) for Node.js allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network' — Important, CVSS 5.9, Exploited: No.

items.title: ID Protection's atypical travel detection is now documented as real-time, not offline, and the 14-day learning period is gone from the page
items.officialTitle: Risk detection and event types — Atypical travel
items.publishedNote: Read from MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs commits f6b02dd237 and 2d2e626c16 (15 October 2026, 19:28 and 19:43 UTC) and confirmed on the published Learn page through the Microsoft Learn MCP server on 16 October 2026.
items.fingerprintBefore: Atypical travel | Offline | Premium | unlikelyTravel. The system has an initial learning period of the earliest of 14 days or 10 logins.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft changed the risk detection table on 15 October 2026: 'Atypical travel' (riskEventType unlikelyTravel, Premium) is now listed as Real-time instead of Offline, and the detail reads 'Calculated in real-time'. The sentence describing an initial learning period of the earliest of 14 days or 10 logins was replaced with 'The system uses adaptive learning to learn a new user's sign-in behavior.'
items.why: A real-time detection raises sign-in risk during the sign-in itself, so a risk-based Conditional Access policy can now challenge or block an atypical-travel sign-in instead of the user being flagged after the fact. Expect more MFA prompts and blocks attributed to unlikelyTravel, and a change in DetectionTimingType in AADUserRiskEvents.
items.action: Review sign-in-risk Conditional Access policies with this in mind, tell the service desk that travelling users may be challenged at sign-in, and trend unlikelyTravel by DetectionTimingType to see when your tenant moves (query in Hunting).

items.title: Entra may now show a risk-based CAPTCHA from Arkose Labs before sending an SMS or placing a voice call for sign-in
items.officialTitle: Risk-based anti-bot verification (CAPTCHA) for telephony-based sign-in
items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.publishedNote: New article added to MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs in commit 856b4a9a64 on 15 October 2026 (its ms.date is 14 October 2026).
items.fingerprint: Microsoft documents that Entra ID may ask a user to complete a risk-based anti-bot verification, such as a CAPTCHA provided by Arkose Labs, before it sends an SMS or places a voice call for sign-in, to limit telephony fraud such as International Revenue Share Fraud. The check is risk-based on client behaviour signals and Microsoft does not publish its criteria; if the dialog does not load, the Arkose Labs domains may need to be allowed. SMS and voice are not removed.
items.why: A user who cannot finish an SMS sign-in may be blocked by a proxy or web filter that drops the Arkose Labs domains, not by an attack. It also confirms that SMS and voice are being abused enough for Microsoft to gate them — another reason to retire them.
items.action: Add the Arkose Labs domains Microsoft lists to your proxy allow list, brief the service desk on the new dialog, and use it as a prompt to move remaining SMS and voice users to Authenticator or passkeys.

items.title: Enterprise app 'Activation status' is now documented: Deactivated can mean tenant sign-in off, the app registration deactivated, or Microsoft disabling the app
items.officialTitle: Properties of an enterprise application — Activation status
items.publishedNote: Read from MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs commit a7fb5f325f, 15 October 2026 11:46 UTC.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft added an 'Activation status' section on 15 October 2026: the enterprise application shows Deactivated if sign-in is disabled for the service principal in the tenant (accountEnabled=false), if the app registration is deactivated (isDisabled=true), or if Microsoft disabled the application (disabledByMicrosoftStatus=DisabledDueToViolationOfServicesAgreement). 'The label alone doesn't identify which condition applies.' Enabling tenant-local sign-in does not override app registration deactivation or Microsoft disablement.
items.why: During a consent-phishing response the label 'Deactivated' is ambiguous: an analyst who sees it may assume Microsoft has already disabled the app, or may re-enable sign-in and believe the app works again. Only the three properties tell which condition applies.
items.action: Update the consent-phishing playbook to read accountEnabled, isDisabled and disabledByMicrosoftStatus through Graph instead of trusting the portal label, and alert when disabledByMicrosoftStatus is set on any service principal in your tenant.
items.docRefNote: The enterprise-apps folder is not among the watched documentation pages of collect_nt.py; the changed lines are quoted in the fingerprint from entra-docs commit a7fb5f325f.

items.title: Intune ends CNAME auto-discovery for Windows MDM-only enrollment on 15 January 2027
items.officialTitle: Intune ending support for Windows MDM-only enrollment CNAME auto-discovery
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft writes: “Starting January 15, 2027, or soon after, Intune will no longer support domain name server (DNS) CNAME-based auto-discovery for Windows MDM-only enrollment scenarios.”
items.fingerprint: From 15 January 2027, or soon after, Windows MDM-only enrollment no longer finds the enrollment service through an EnterpriseEnrollment DNS CNAME record; users must enter https://enrollment.manage.microsoft.com/enrollmentserver/discovery.svc when prompted. Enrollment through Microsoft Entra ID or other identity platforms, and devices already enrolled, are not affected.
items.why: A stale EnterpriseEnrollment CNAME that nobody owns is a record an attacker could point elsewhere; once discovery stops using it, it can be removed.
items.action: Find out whether any Windows MDM-only enrollment still relies on the CNAME, update the enrollment instructions before January, and remove the EnterpriseEnrollment record once nothing uses it.

items.title: Office LTSC 2021, Visio LTSC 2021 and Project LTSC 2021 left support on 13 October 2026 — no more security updates
items.officialTitle: Support for Office LTSC 2021 and additional apps ended on October 13, 2026
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft writes: “support for Office LTSC 2021 ended on October 13, 2026.”
items.fingerprint: Support for Office LTSC 2021, Visio LTSC 2021, Project LTSC 2021 and several other products ended on 13 October 2026: no more security updates, bug fixes or technical support. The applications keep working. Microsoft recommends Microsoft 365 Apps, or Office LTSC 2024 (supported to October 2029) for disconnected scenarios.
items.why: The 30 Office CVEs Microsoft added on 15 October are the kind of Word and Outlook RCE that an unsupported Office 2021 install will never be fixed for again.
items.action: Query your software inventory for Office, Visio and Project LTSC 2021 builds and put every one on a dated upgrade plan; treat any left after November as an exposure in the vulnerability register.

items.title: Edge 159 switches browser-native XSLT off by default from mid-December; the temporary XSLTEnabled policy goes in Edge 176
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Edge: Browser-native XSLT will be disabled by default
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft gives no exact day: “We will begin rolling out in mid-December 2026”, Edge 159 Stable; the XSLTEnabled policy is planned for removal in Edge 176 in Summer 2027.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft Edge 159 disables the XSLTProcessor JavaScript API and XML processing instructions that reference XSLT stylesheets by default, rolling out from mid-December 2026, to remove an aging native code path that processes untrusted XML and XSLT. A temporary XSLTEnabled policy restores it until Edge 176 in Summer 2027. Microsoft gives a Lighthouse procedure to find affected pages.
items.why: Removing an attack surface is welcome, but internal portals and appliance web interfaces that render XML with XSLT break — the RD Web Access case (MC1491832) is one already on this page.
items.action: Run the Lighthouse check on internal and appliance web consoles before December, and if you deploy XSLTEnabled, scope it to the sites that need it and track its removal date.

items.title: Teams admins can customise the extensions Weaponizable File Protection blocks from November — and lose Microsoft's list updates if they do
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Teams: Customize file extensions blocked by Weaponizable File Protection
items.deadlineNote: Rollout “Beginning in early November 2026 and expected to complete by mid-November 2026.”
items.fingerprint: From early to mid-November 2026 admins can define which file extensions Weaponizable File Protection blocks in Teams, or keep the Microsoft-recommended list. A tenant that customises the list 'will no longer automatically receive future updates to the Microsoft-recommended list'; resetting to the default resumes them.
items.why: A custom list freezes the tenant's protection at the day it was saved: a file type Microsoft adds later because it is being used in Teams phishing will not be blocked.
items.action: Keep the Microsoft list unless a business case forces a change; if you customise, record it and review the list against Microsoft's at least quarterly.

items.title: Teams meetings can take deepfake-detection signals from certified third-party providers from mid-November
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Teams: Third-party synthetic audio and video detection in meetings
items.deadlineNote: Targeted Release from mid-November 2026; General Availability <del>late November to mid-December 2026</del> <ins>will be communicated via Message center</ins> (revised 22 Oct 2026).
items.fingerprint: Teams will integrate certified third-party synthetic audio and video detection solutions that analyse meeting media and send detection signals to Teams; detection is done by the provider, Teams surfaces the signal. Admins deploy the provider app in the Teams admin center, grant its permissions and configure meeting policies. Roadmap ID 573451.
items.why: Voice and video impersonation of executives and help-desk staff is a live social-engineering technique; this gives a control point inside the meeting, but it also hands meeting audio and video to a third party whose data handling you must review.
items.action: If deepfake-assisted social engineering is in your threat model, shortlist providers, review their data processing terms with privacy, and plan which meeting policies (external, executive) get the integration first.

items.title: EmailPostDeliveryEvents gains an ApproverUpn column naming who approved a post-delivery remediation
items.officialTitle: What's new in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 — New ApproverUpn field in the EmailPostDeliveryEvents table
items.publishedNote: Added to the Defender for Office 365 what's new page dated 15 October 2026 (merill/defender-docs-mirror commit ca11cbf, 17:55 UTC). The EmailPostDeliveryEvents schema page read on 16 October 2026 does not list the column yet.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft's Defender for Office 365 what's new page, dated 15 October 2026: 'The EmailPostDeliveryEvents table in Microsoft Defender XDR Advanced Hunting now includes the ApproverUpn field. This field identifies the user or administrator who approved a remediation action.' The table's own schema page does not yet list ApproverUpn.
items.why: Who approved a soft-delete or move of delivered mail was only in the Action center; having it in hunting lets you audit manual remediation and catch an approval made by an account that should not be approving.
items.action: Add ApproverUpn to any post-delivery remediation report and run the hunting query in this brief to list approvals by approver; use column_ifexists until the column reaches your tenant.

items.title: Vulnerability assessment for Microsoft Store applications is generally available in Defender Vulnerability Management
items.officialTitle: What's new in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint — Vulnerability assessment for Microsoft Store applications (GA)
items.publishedNote: Moved from Preview to an October 2026 GA row on the MDE what's new page dated 14 October 2026 (merill/defender-docs-mirror commit 33875d2, 15 October 12:50 UTC).
items.fingerprintBefore: Preview: You can now monitor vulnerabilities on devices running Microsoft Store applications, including Microsoft Teams, Mozilla Firefox, WhatsApp, Slack, Dropbox …
items.fingerprint: Microsoft moved 'Vulnerability assessment for Microsoft Store applications' from Preview to GA in the October 2026 section of the Defender for Endpoint what's new page: Defender Vulnerability Management detects supported Microsoft Store applications, adds them to the software inventory and assesses them for vulnerabilities. Coverage is limited to a select set of commonly used applications; the Software evidence area shows the file path.
items.why: Store-installed Teams, Firefox, Slack or WhatsApp were a blind spot in software inventory; GA means their CVEs now count in exposure score and recommendations, so numbers may rise without any new install.
items.action: Expect exposure-score movement on devices with Store apps; check the software inventory for Store-installed browsers and messengers and decide whether they are allowed.

items.tier0Note: UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All writes the certificate identifiers that certificate-based authentication uses to map a certificate to a user, and AdministrativeUnitMember.ReadWrite.All moves accounts in and out of a delegated administrator's scope: both are tier-0 paths.
items.title: Twelve more Graph permissions became grantable, among them UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All, which can bind a certificate to any user, and AdministrativeUnitMember.ReadWrite.All
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Graph service principal: application roles and delegated scopes (merill/microsoft-info daily export)
items.reference: no MC/RM post — service principal only
items.fingerprint: Between the 15 October (d1292fc, 20:27 UTC) and the 16 October (5d64224, 20:00 UTC) dumps of the Microsoft Graph service principal, application roles went from 762 to 769 and delegated scopes from 847 to 859, nothing removed. New application roles: AdministrativeUnit.ReadBasic.All, AdministrativeUnit.ReadWriteBasic.All, AdministrativeUnitMember.ReadWrite.All, CrossTenantIdentityMapping.Read.All, CrossTenantIdentityMapping.ReadWrite.All, Policy.Read.SecurityDefaults and UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All ('Allows the app to update certificate user IDs for all users, without a signed-in user'). The same seven plus CopilotCostManagement.Read.All, CopilotCostManagement-CreditReq.Read.All and .ReadWrite.All, Repository.Read.All and Repository.ReadWrite.All arrive as admin-consent delegated scopes. None is on the permissions reference (unchanged since 8 October).
items.why: UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All lets an application rewrite certificateUserIds, the values certificate-based authentication uses to decide which user a certificate signs in as: where certificate-based authentication is enabled, an app holding it can point a certificate issued by a CA the tenant trusts at any account, a Global Administrator included (inferred from how CBA user binding works; Microsoft's text says only that it updates certificate user IDs). It is grantable in every tenant from today and documented nowhere, so no consent review checklist names it yet.
items.action: Add the GUIDs 10d0f892-6ef8-4cd8-9f4c-614345762e90 (application) and 01d92422-30dd-4401-a504-aa0a84c463bc (delegated) of UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All and 9205f977-63a7-4c23-9d0c-8051235b0e4c / 14f19140-a110-48da-b3ba-63c2862bb7da of AdministrativeUnitMember.ReadWrite.All to the consent alert list today; alert on any change to certificateUserIds in the audit log.

items.title: Exchange Online stops returning selected properties from Get-Mailbox -Migration on 15 November and blocks setting them through New-Mailbox -Migration on 15 December
items.officialTitle: Action required: Review property changes for Exchange Online scenarios
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft's actionRequiredByDateTime is 15 November 2026; the second phase, blocking configuration through New-Mailbox -Migration, begins 15 December 2026. The body also says 'beginning November 10, 2026' in one example sentence.
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 16 October 2026. As part of Exchange Online directory modernization Microsoft deprecates selected properties returned or used by Get-Mailbox -Migration and New-Mailbox -Migration. From 15 November 2026 the properties are no longer returned in those responses; from 15 December 2026 they can no longer be configured through New-Mailbox -Migration. The property list is in the linked Microsoft documentation, not in the post.
items.why: Mailbox-migration and onboarding scripts that read these properties will get empty values without an error, so a provisioning or audit job can silently produce wrong output.
items.action: Search automation, runbooks and third-party migration tools for Get-Mailbox -Migration and New-Mailbox -Migration before 15 November, compare the properties they read with Microsoft's list, and test the scripts against a tenant where the change has landed.

items.title: Microsoft cancels the EWS block for Kiosk, F1 and F3 mailboxes that was due on 1 October 2026
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Update to EWS Access for Kiosk / Frontline Worker Licenses
items.deadlineNote: The post previously named 1 October 2026 (moved from 30 June) as the date EWS requests from these licences would get HTTP 403. The 16 October update withdraws it; no new date is given.
items.fingerprint: Updated 16 October 2026: 'We have decided not to move forward with this change.' The post had said that from 1 October 2026 EWS access would be blocked, with HTTP 403, for mailboxes licensed only with Exchange Online Kiosk or Microsoft 365 / Office 365 F1 or F3, because those licences never carried EWS rights although the restriction was never enforced.
items.fingerprintBefore: From 1 October 2026 (previously 30 June) EWS requests from mailboxes licensed only with Exchange Online Kiosk, F1 or F3 get HTTP 403; assign a licence with EWS rights to keep access.
items.why: Frontline mailboxes keep EWS access, so an EWS client or a token stolen from a Kiosk or F3 user still reaches the mailbox. A licence change made to prepare for the block is no longer needed; the EWSAllowedAppIDs allow list is now the control that limits EWS.
items.action: Do not rely on licensing to keep EWS away from frontline mailboxes. Restrict EWS with EWSAllowedAppIDs and EWSEnabled per mailbox where frontline users do not need it, and keep EWS sign-ins from F-licensed users in your hunting queries.

items.title: SharePoint and OneDrive .agent agents stop working after March 2027; new agents move to the Copilot Agent Builder from mid-November
items.officialTitle: Upcoming changes to Agents in SharePoint and OneDrive
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft writes that agents using the .agent file format 'will continue to work across SharePoint, Teams, and Copilot app until the end of March 2027'; new agents use the Copilot Agent Builder from mid-November 2026. No single action date.
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 16 October 2026. SharePoint and OneDrive agents built on the .agent file format are being moved into the Microsoft Copilot extensibility ecosystem, the Copilot app home experience (MC1479277) and the Microsoft plugin registry (MC1484008). From mid-November 2026 new agents are created with the Copilot Agent Builder; .agent files keep working in SharePoint, Teams and the Copilot app until the end of March 2027, after which they stop. Owners can use Copilot in SharePoint, convert the .agent file to a skill, or upgrade the agent.
items.why: Site agents move from a file sitting in a document library to an object governed through the plugin registry, so whoever reviews which agents can read which sites has to look in a new place, and abandoned .agent files will simply stop.
items.action: Inventory .agent files in SharePoint and OneDrive, name an owner for each, and decide before March 2027 which to convert; review who may publish to the plugin registry.

items.title: The Copilot Studio app in Teams is retired by February 2027; editing agents there ends in January
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Copilot Studio – Teams app retirement
items.deadlineNote: Editing in the Teams app ends in January 2027 and the app is removed from Teams in February 2027; rollout early January to early February 2027. No single day is stated.
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 16 October 2026. Agent creation in the Copilot Studio app in Teams is already no longer supported. From January 2027 existing classic-style chatbot agents can no longer be edited in the Teams app, and from February 2027 the app is no longer available in Teams. Agents keep working and are managed at copilotstudio.microsoft.com.
items.why: Agents built by business users in Teams keep running but are managed only in the web app afterwards; an ownership review should happen while the creators still know what they built.
items.action: List Copilot Studio agents created from Teams, confirm each has an owner who can reach the web app, and update user guidance before January 2027.

items.title: Teams voicemail emails move the caller from the From field to the Subject and can be sent from your own domain from March 2027
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Teams: Upcoming change to voicemail message delivery by email
items.deadlineNote: General availability is estimated to begin in early March 2027 and complete by late June 2027; Microsoft says the schedule may change and a further post will confirm it.
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 16 October 2026. To let organisations send voicemail notifications from their own domain under their SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain-protection policies, Teams gets a new voicemail email delivery solution: the From field will no longer carry the caller's name, number or address, which move to the Subject and stay in the body, and the sender address supports Bring Your Own Domain. Rollout is estimated from early March to late June 2027. Microsoft states no new compliance requirements.
items.why: Mail-flow rules, journaling and phishing filters that key on the voicemail sender or the caller in From will stop matching; voicemail mail from your own domain is also something an attacker can imitate if DMARC is not enforced.
items.action: Find transport rules and filters that match Teams voicemail by sender or From, plan their change for March 2027, and enforce DMARC on the domain you choose for voicemail.

items.title: Insider Risk Management alerts in Defender XDR slip from September 2026 to February 2027 (roadmap)
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Purview: Insider Risk Management- IRM alerts in XDR
items.deadlineNote: Roadmap release February CY2027 (September CY2026 until 16 October 2026, June CY2026 before 11 June); a target, not a deadline.
items.fingerprint: Roadmap 560075, status In development, release phase General Availability. On 16 October 2026 its release date moved from September CY2026 to February CY2027. IRM alerts are to appear in the Defender XDR unified alert and incident queue; IRM alerts, indicators and enriched events in advanced hunting and through Graph API, enabled by 'Share data with Microsoft Defender XDR' in IRM settings. IRM data in Defender XDR does not honour anonymization.
items.why: A SOC that planned to correlate insider-risk alerts with Defender incidents and hunt them in KQL this autumn has to wait until February 2027 at the earliest; until then IRM stays a separate queue.
items.action: Keep the IRM-to-SOC hand-off as it is today and move any plan that assumed IRM alerts in the Defender incident queue to February 2027; when it ships, decide who may see de-anonymized IRM data in Defender before switching on the sharing setting.

items.title: Dataverse audit events reach Purview without customer data: before-and-after column values stay in Dataverse only
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Power Platform governance and administration: Security and compliance - Prevent sending sensitive data to Purview audit logs
items.deadlineNote: Roadmap entry created 16 October 2026 with status Launched, release June CY2026, Worldwide.
items.fingerprint: Roadmap 576863, created 16 October 2026, status Launched, General Availability, release June CY2026, Worldwide. 'All customer data is removed before these audit events are sent to Purview activity logging.' Dataverse audit logs still capture create and update events with a column's before-and-after values, but those values are not sent to Purview activity logging.
items.why: An investigation that searches the Purview audit log for what a user changed in a Dataverse record now finds the event without the values; the evidence has to be pulled from Dataverse auditing, which has its own retention.
items.action: Update Power Platform investigation runbooks to read before-and-after values from Dataverse audit history, and check Dataverse audit retention covers your investigation window.

items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.title: Deleting an Entra custom role now soft-deletes it, and Graph v1.0 can list, restore or permanently delete soft-deleted custom roles
items.officialTitle: unifiedRoleDefinition: delete; unifiedRoleDefinition: restore; directoryRoleManagementDeletedItemContainer
items.fingerprint: Microsoft documented in v1.0 on 16 October 2026: 'Deleting an active custom role definition soft-deletes it. You can then restore the role or permanently delete it from the deleted-items collection. This feature requires a Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 license.' New: GET /roleManagement/directory/deletedItems/roleDefinitions, POST …/roleDefinitions/{id}/restore and DELETE /roleManagement/directory/deletedItems/roleDefinitions/{id}; least privileged permission RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory.
items.why: A deleted custom role can come back with its permissions: someone holding RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can restore a role you removed, and a 'delete' in the audit log is no longer the end of that role.
items.action: Alert on restore and permanent delete of role definitions in the Entra audit log alongside create and update, and include soft-deleted custom roles in privileged-role reviews.

items.title: Graph v1.0 gains a device provision action that lets approved VDI providers create devices in a customer directory
items.officialTitle: device: provision
items.fingerprint: Microsoft's Graph what's new for October 2026, added 16 October: 'Added the provision action to the device resource in v1.0 to enable approved Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI) providers to provision devices in a customer's directory.'
items.why: A third party can now write device objects into the tenant through a supported API; device-based Conditional Access trusts those objects, so who is approved to call it matters.
items.action: Find which VDI provider applications hold consent in your tenant and watch the Entra audit log for device creations by those service principals.

items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.title: Defender XDR multitenant Unified RBAC: creating, deleting and importing custom roles across tenants is no longer preview
items.officialTitle: Multitenant Unified RBAC in Microsoft Defender XDR
items.fingerprint: On 16 October 2026 the headings 'Create or edit a custom role (Preview)', 'Delete roles (Preview)' and 'Import roles (Preview)' lost the Preview label on the multitenant Unified RBAC page: role definitions managed from a managing tenant and pushed to managed tenants are a supported feature.
items.why: One change in the managing tenant now lands in every managed tenant by design, so the people who can create or import roles there hold the keys to every customer's Defender permissions.
items.action: List who in the managing tenant can create, edit and import multitenant roles, and require review of every role import.

items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.title: Sentinel permissions in Defender Unified RBAC can now be assigned to GDAP user groups; service principals still cannot
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Defender XDR Unified role-based access control (RBAC)
items.fingerprint: On 16 October 2026 Microsoft changed 'Assigning permissions to a service principal or to a GDAP user group in Microsoft Sentinel isn't supported in unified RBAC' to 'Assigning permissions to a GDAP user group in Microsoft Sentinel is supported in unified RBAC' and 'Assigning permissions to a service principal isn't supported in unified RBAC'.
items.fingerprintBefore: Assigning permissions to a service principal or to a GDAP user group in Microsoft Sentinel isn't supported in unified RBAC.
items.why: A partner's GDAP group can now hold Sentinel permissions through Unified RBAC, which widens who outside the tenant can read or change Sentinel data once Sentinel is activated in Unified RBAC.
items.action: Review GDAP relationships and their groups before activating Sentinel in Unified RBAC; keep automation service principals on Azure RBAC.

items.title: Defender real-time protection for AI agents names four threat scenarios it can block: malicious content, secret exfiltration, evasion and unsafe email domains
items.officialTitle: Real-time protection for AI agents
items.fingerprint: A 'Supported threat scenarios' section was added on 16 October 2026: Malicious content propagation, Secret exfiltration ('an agent interaction exposes or attempts to transfer secrets, such as API keys, credentials, or access tokens'), Evasion techniques and Unsafe email domain. With blocking enabled each is blocked across user requests, model responses, tool requests and tool responses; unsafe email domain is evaluated at the tool request.
items.why: It tells the SOC which agent-abuse cases a blocking rule actually covers; prompt injection that does not fall into one of the four is not claimed.
items.action: Turn on blocking for secret exfiltration and unsafe email domain first, and keep detection-only for the others until you have reviewed a week of alerts.

items.title: Critical remote code execution in the Windows Raw Image Extension is fixed through a Microsoft Store update, not Windows Update
items.officialTitle: Windows Raw Image Extension Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
items.fingerprint: MSRC published CVE-2026-96202 on 16 October 2026: Critical, CVSS 8.8, heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Raw Image Extension; a user must open a crafted file. Fixed in Raw Image Extension 2.4.36.0 and 2.5.35.0, delivered through the Microsoft Store. Not exploited, not publicly disclosed.
items.why: Devices where Store updates are blocked or managed never receive the fix through the monthly patch, so a vulnerability dashboard fed by Windows Update shows them as clean.
items.action: Query the installed Raw Image Extension version across Windows devices and push 2.4.36.0 / 2.5.35.0 where the Store does not update apps.

items.title: Four Microsoft-assigned remote code execution CVEs in Edge published on 16 October
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
items.fingerprint: MSRC published CVE-2026-85890, CVE-2026-85897, CVE-2026-96198 and CVE-2026-96199 on 16 October 2026, each 'Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability', Important, not exploited, alongside the Chromium CVEs listed in the MSRC feed the same day. The entries do not state the fixed Edge build.
items.why: Edge RCEs are fixed only once the browser restarts on the new build; a fleet that defers browser restarts stays exposed after the update has downloaded.
items.action: Confirm managed devices run the current Edge stable build and that the relaunch notification policy forces a restart within your patch window.

items.title: Defender for Cloud replaces the Resource Graph query that finds SQL servers protected through Azure Monitor Agent

items.title: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM external key management is generally available in all public regions

For organizations with regulatory or sovereignty requirements to retain physical control of key-encryption keys, it lets Azure services that su[pport customer-managed keys use them].' The update text is truncated in the feed.

items.action: Where you adopt it, add the external HSM to monitoring and to the recovery runbook; losing it makes the protected data unreadable.

items.title: Defender for Identity: existing customers get a 30-day banner, after which sensor v3.x activation and Windows auditing are switched on even where the setting is Off, unless you opt out in the banner
items.officialTitle: Automatic sensor v3.x activation and Windows auditing for existing customers
items.publishedNote: Microsoft prints the entry under 'October 2026' with no day; the page's ms.date moved from 2026-10-06 to 2026-10-18 in this brief's mirror commit 9ec4cfe (18 October 2026, 22:22 UTC), and the live page was read through the Microsoft Learn MCP server in this run.
items.deadlineNote: No date: the banner runs 30 days from whenever a tenant is included in the rollout, which Microsoft calls very gradual.
items.tier0Note: Activates the sensor capability and rewrites Windows audit policy on domain controllers, AD FS, AD CS and Entra Connect servers onboarded to Defender for Endpoint, including where an administrator had set the toggle to Off.
items.fingerprint: New October 2026 entry on the Defender for Identity what's new page: 'This rollout applies only to organizations that are licensed for Defender for Identity and have an active workspace. Eligible organizations included in the rollout see a banner on the Sensor management tab of the On-premises settings page for 30 days. After the 30-day notice period, Automatic sensor v3.x activation and Automatic Windows auditing configuration are enabled by default through a very gradual rollout, including settings currently set to Off. To keep your current settings, select Opt out in the banner during the notice period.' The September entry was rewritten to the same wording.
items.fingerprintBefore: Existing Defender for Identity customers: The change becomes available gradually. The Defender portal displays a notice before it enables the settings automatically. After the notice period ends, the portal enables the settings.
items.why: A toggle an administrator turned Off is no longer a decision that holds: unless someone clicks Opt out inside a 30-day banner, the portal activates the sensor and changes audit policy on tier-0 servers. A tenant whose change control relies on the Off setting will see an unapproved change on its domain controllers.
items.action: Check the Sensor management tab under Settings > Identities > On-premises in every tenant you run for the banner; decide before the 30 days end whether to opt out or enable deliberately, and record the decision in change control for the domain controllers, AD FS, AD CS and Entra Connect servers.

items.title: Microsoft's Graph permission file gains seven permissions on 16 and 17 October, among them CredentialProvenance.ReadWrite.All, HardDeletionSetting.ReadWrite.Enable and PrivilegedAccess-CustomExt.ReadWrite.All
items.officialTitle: Weekly Permissions sync 2026-10-16 and 2026-10-17 (microsoftgraph/microsoft-graph-devx-content, daily branches)
items.officialTitleNote: The commit subjects of the two daily branches; Microsoft published no announcement.
items.reference: no MC/RM post — permission file only
items.publishedNote: Dates of the daily branches permissions-update/2026-10-16 (commit d723f8c) and permissions-update/2026-10-17 (commit 0cd056d), read by collect_graph_diff.py in this run; neither branch is merged to master.
items.tier0Note: CredentialProvenance.ReadWrite.All (privilege level 4) attests the provenance of a user's authentication methods; HardDeletionSetting.ReadWrite.Enable is mapped to PATCH on users, groups, applications and service principals.
items.fingerprint: 16 October (d723f8c): CredentialProvenance.ReadWrite.All (level 4; PATCH /users/{id}/authentication/provenance, POST /users/{id}/authentication/methods/{id}/attestProvenance), HardDeletionSetting.ReadWrite.Enable (level 3; PATCH /users/{id}, /groups/{id}, /applications/{id}, /serviceprincipals/{id}), IdentityVerification.Read, .Read.All and .ReadWrite.All (level 4; /users/{id}/identityVerificationStatus and its verificationEvents, including block and unblock). 17 October (0cd056d): PrivilegedAccess-CustomExt.Read.All and .ReadWrite.All (level 3; /identityGovernance/privilegedAccess/customExtensions), and AuditLog.Read.All gains GET /auditlogs/resourcepolicy. All seven were already in the catalog from the deployment map; none is on the permissions reference.
items.why: These are the endpoints an app with the permission can call once consent is granted: one writes the provenance attestation of authentication methods, one can switch on hard deletion for users, groups, applications and service principals (no recycle bin to restore from), and the PIM custom-extension pair can change what runs when a role is activated.
items.action: Add the seven names to the consent-review watch list and alert on any grant of CredentialProvenance.ReadWrite.All, HardDeletionSetting.ReadWrite.Enable or PrivilegedAccess-CustomExt.ReadWrite.All; nothing to change until an app requests them.

items.title: CVE-2026-70197 (.NET remote code execution, CVSS 8.1): Microsoft now says the October fix does not address the vulnerability and a complete mitigation is still being prepared
items.officialTitle: .NET Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
items.publishedNote: MSRC Security Update Guide API, CVE-2026-70197: released 13 October 2026, latest revision 19 October 2026, read 20 October 2026.
items.fingerprint: CVE-2026-70197, an out-of-bounds write in .NET that lets an unauthorized attacker execute code over a network (Important, CVSS 8.1, Exploited: No, Publicly disclosed: No), was published on 13 October 2026. The revision of 19 October 2026 reads: 'Microsoft is aware that the vulnerability for which this CVE was assigned has not been addressed. We are working to prepare and test a complete mitigation. We will update this document when there is more information.'
items.fingerprintBefore: Information published 13 October 2026; KB article links for .NET 11.0 and Visual Studio added 15 October; acknowledgement updated 16 October.
items.why: A patch-compliance report that shows the October .NET update installed now overstates protection: Microsoft states the installed fix does not close the flaw, so .NET services reachable from the network stay exposed until a new update ships.
items.action: Do not close the CVE-2026-70197 ticket on the October update alone; list internet-facing .NET services, keep them behind the WAF and network restrictions you already have, and watch the MSRC page for the replacement update.

items.title: Exchange Online: users can send from any of their mailbox's aliases once an admin turns it on (generally available)
items.officialTitle: Sending from Aliases
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 19 October 2026: sending from aliases is generally available in Exchange Online, so users can send mail from any proxy address of their mailbox; admins enable it through PowerShell or the Exchange admin center.
items.why: Once enabled, the From address of outbound mail can be any alias rather than the primary address, so DLP rules, transport rules and hunting queries that match on the primary SMTP address miss mail sent from an alias.
items.action: Before enabling it, review transport and DLP rules and advanced hunting queries on EmailEvents that key on SenderFromAddress for the primary address only, and decide whether aliases should be allowed tenant-wide.

items.officialTitle: External Recipients Banner on Outlook Mobile

items.officialTitle: Microsoft Purview | eDiscovery: In-product diagnostics to troubleshoot common challenges
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 19 October 2026: three read-only diagnostics in Purview eDiscovery for case access, security filters and hold-policy distribution, rolling out from October 2026 to February 2027; they do not change configuration.

items.officialTitle: Viva Glint: Service Admin role will have access to all report attributes
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 19 October 2026: starting 17 November 2026 the Viva Glint Service Admin role has unrestricted access to all report attributes, removing earlier restrictions; Microsoft asks organisations to review role assignments and use narrower roles where needed.

items.title: Microsoft Security Blog: Defender agent discovery grows to 60 agent types, plus Guardian Agents, Dynamic Permissions and Conditional Access for agents under Project Perception
items.officialTitle: Agents are your newest insiders. Security must move at their speed.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft Security Blog post of 19 October 2026: Defender agent discovery adds 35 local agent types for 60 in all (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot among them); Entra Agent ID gains identity types for local and previously unknown agents; Project Perception adds Guardian Agents and playbooks, the Microsoft Execution Container sandbox, Dynamic Permissions, Dynamic Agent Risk and dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The post states no GA or preview status for any of them.

items.action: Ask the endpoint team whether Defender's agent inventory is visible in your tenant and compare it with the coding agents you know are installed; plan nothing on the undated controls until Microsoft publishes their status.

items.title: Exchange Online: the Change Optics report, which shows the traffic an upcoming service change would affect, is generally available
items.officialTitle: The Change Optics Report is now Generally Available in Exchange Online

items.action: Have the messaging team open the report and check which of your connectors or senders it lists before the next Exchange enforcement date.

items.title: Entra makes Choose Your Own Telephony Provider generally available on 30 October; Microsoft-provided SMS and voice still retire 1 February 2027 (Global Administrators and external users 1 July 2027)
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Entra: Choose your own telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication
items.tier0Note: Authentication method for every account still on SMS or voice, Global Administrators included until 1 July 2027.
items.fingerprint: From 30 October 2026 organizations can configure a supported third-party telephony provider, bought through Microsoft Security Store, to deliver SMS and voice authentication while Entra ID keeps enforcing the authentication method policies. Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication retires on 1 February 2027 for all users except Global Administrators and external users (1 July 2027); after that, users whose only MFA method is SMS or voice get a blocking passkey registration prompt unless a provider is configured. Purchasing requires an Azure billing subscription and resource group.
items.why: A third party now sits in the MFA delivery path for every user it covers, and the 1 February 2027 retirement turns any account still relying only on SMS or voice into a blocking passkey prompt at sign-in.
items.action: Count the users whose only MFA method is SMS or voice, move them to passkeys or Authenticator before 1 February 2027, and buy a provider only for a documented residual population, with the provider treated as a tier-0 supplier.

items.title: Teams adds AI-based phishing and social-engineering detection to external first-contact chats: Targeted Release early to mid-November, worldwide early to mid-December
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Teams: Phishing detection for messaging
items.fingerprint: Teams analyses conversation context to detect phishing, social engineering, impersonation and deceptive intent that carry no malicious link or file. Targeted Release early to mid-November 2026, general availability early to mid-December 2026. For most users detection covers external first-contact chats; Teams mobile users in China may also get it on in-tenant conversations. Detection may first run silently during quality validation; afterwards users see a warning. No admin action or configuration; message content is not retained for training.

items.action: Tell the helpdesk and users what the warning looks like before mid-November, and route user reports of Teams chats into the Defender submissions queue so a warning a user dismisses still reaches an analyst.

items.title: Copilot Code reaches Frontier users from late October: users build and publish apps grounded on Work IQ data, cloud coding on by default, local coding and GitHub off until an admin enables them
items.officialTitle: Copilot Code is rolling out in Frontier
items.fingerprint: Copilot Code starts in the Frontier program in late October 2026 for users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence and a spending policy. items.title: Storm-0940 used the ARTEX agentic framework and compromised ConnectWise multi-tenant apps to act app-only in customer tenants; one app self-assigned Global Administrator
items.officialTitle: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise
items.reference: no MC/RM post — Microsoft Security Blog
items.tier0Note: A compromised multi-tenant app with existing consent self-assigned Global Administrator in a customer tenant.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise multi-tenant application compromise (ConnectWise advisory of 16 October 2026) to Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, which used the open-source multi-agent framework ARTEX from September 2026. Attackers controlled the identities of ConnectWise cloud apps (Cloud Backup, MS Teams, MS Graph) and authenticated app-only to customer tenants, with reconnaissance, credential additions, changes to identities, groups and privileged roles; one app self-assigned Global Administrator. ARTEX-driven sign-in attempts reached more than 2,250 tenants. Microsoft publishes app IDs 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 and 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827, IPs in 144.172.64.0/24, Defender XDR and Defender for Cloud Apps alert names and hunting queries; it states the activity did not stem from a Microsoft vulnerability.
items.why: An app your tenant consented to years ago acted as the attacker with no user sign-in and no MFA prompt; the review window Microsoft asks for starts 1 October, so logs with shorter retention are already losing the evidence.
items.action: Search every tenant by application ID, keep the ConnectWise apps disabled without deleting them, export service principal sign-ins, Graph activity and Entra audit from 1 October, and review credential additions, app-role assignments and role changes made by those service principals.

items.title: Exchange Online starts turning EWS off: the Exchange team says deprecation begins now, blocked EWS apps can be unblocked only until April 2027
items.officialTitle: EWS Deprecation Is Here – What This Means To You
items.reference: no MC/RM post — Exchange Team Blog and Microsoft Learn
items.fingerprint: The Exchange Team Blog posted on 21 October 2026 that EWS deprecation in Exchange Online is starting, with a second post on temporarily unblocking blocked EWS applications until April 2027. Microsoft Learn states EWS starts to be disabled globally from October 2026 and is fully and permanently disabled on 1 April 2027; tenants that did not opt in had EwsEnabled moved from null to false, and setting EwsEnabled back to null (Set-OrganizationConfig) is a temporary workaround that stops working at the final disablement. The blog bodies render only in a browser and were read here through their descriptions; the dates come from the Learn pages.
items.why: Every EWS application still in use, Apple Mail and Calendar on macOS and classic Outlook for Mac among them, either breaks now or survives on a temporary exception that re-opens the protocol Midnight Blizzard used; the exception expires on 1 April 2027 regardless.
items.action: Pull the EWS usage report, list the apps by App ID, decide per app whether it gets a temporary entry in the EWS allowed App IDs list, and alert on any change to EwsEnabled or EwsAllowedAppIDs in the Exchange admin audit log.
items.deadlineNote: 1 April 2027 is the permanent disablement date stated on Microsoft Learn.

items.title: Entra ID Protection documents a new real-time risk detection, Suspicious credential addition (riskEventType suspiciousCredentialAddition), for an authentication method added under suspicious circumstances
items.officialTitle: What are risk detections? — Suspicious credential addition
items.fingerprint: The risk detections page gained a premium, real-time user risk detection on 19 October 2026 (entra-docs 8d54ff26da) with its riskEventType written as TBD; on 21 October 2026 (82e232b313, ms.date 10/21/2026) the riskEventType became suspiciousCredentialAddition. Microsoft's text: the detection identifies when a new authentication method is added to an account under suspicious circumstances, which might indicate that an attacker accessed the account and registered a new credential; calculated in real time; requires Microsoft Entra ID P2. No rollout date or preview label is stated on the page.
items.why: Registering a second authentication method is how an account takeover becomes persistent; a real-time risk on that step can drive a user-risk Conditional Access policy before the attacker's own method is used.
items.action: Add suspiciousCredentialAddition to the riskEventType lists your Sentinel and Defender rules match on, check that user-risk policies require remediation for it, and review the first detections against the AuditLogs 'User registered security info' events.

items.title: Entra documents Microsoft-initiated revocation of compromised app credentials: tokenRevocations on applications and service principals, issuer 0e0fb671-b107-448b-a273-9d0ded7627a7
items.officialTitle: Troubleshoot revoked application credentials
items.tier0Note: Application and service-principal credentials are the app-only path into a tenant; a revocation Microsoft issues is a compromise signal on that path.
items.fingerprint: A new Learn article (ms.date 22 October 2026) says Microsoft can revoke an application credential after detecting that a threat actor compromised it; revocations are recorded in a beta tokenRevocations collection on both the application and the service principal, a Microsoft-issued one carries auditDetails.issuedBy 0e0fb671-b107-448b-a273-9d0ded7627a7, and the audit log shows an Update application or Update service principal event initiated by Azure Active Directory Protection Services; token requests fail with AADSTS700027, AADSTS7005003, AADSTS7005004, AADSTS7005005 or AADSTS7005006.
items.why: A workload that suddenly fails with one of these AADSTS codes may be the first sign that Microsoft saw its secret or certificate in an attacker's hands; deleting the revocation to make the error go away re-opens the credential, and tokens already issued can keep working for up to 24 hours on some resources.
items.action: Add the five AADSTS codes and the initiator Azure Active Directory Protection Services on Update application / Update service principal to detections; treat a Microsoft-issued revocation as an incident, rotate the credential and remove anything the attacker added, and never delete the revocation as a fix.

items.title: Perception.Read.All and Perception.Manage.All enter Microsoft's permission file with 18 beta /security/agenticSecurity paths (playbooks, sessions, agent runs)

The same sync maps new endpoints onto six existing permissions.

items.title: Microsoft Graph gains beta APIs for Copilot credit balances, spending policies, threshold alerts and approving users' credit requests
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Graph APIs for Copilot cost management
items.fingerprint: Public preview on the Graph beta endpoint from mid-October 2026: retrieve Copilot credit balances per tenant, user and service; create, update and delete credit spending policies and assign security groups to them; set email alerts on credit thresholds; retrieve, approve or reject end-user credit requests. The post names no endpoint paths or permission scopes; detailed consumption reporting is not included. No action required if the APIs are not used.
items.why: Spending policies and request approvals become writable by any app holding the matching permission; the CopilotCostManagement-* scopes this catalog already tracks are what such an app will ask for.
items.action: Decide who may automate Copilot spending policies; review any consent request for CopilotCostManagement-* scopes as an administrative grant, not a reporting one.

items.title: Microsoft Authenticator gets a new home page, account-restoration banner and guidance, and on Android a battery-optimization prompt; push and passwordless restore improves
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Authenticator: Usability improvements for iOS and Android
items.fingerprint: Rolling out on iOS and Android from October 2026, complete November 2026 (Worldwide, GCC, GCC High, DoD): refreshed home page (Android in November), a banner for accounts not yet restored, clearer first-run restoration guidance, an app-rating prompt during sign-in on iOS, improved restoration for push and passwordless sign-in (iOS first, Android in January 2027), and on Android a non-blocking prompt after sign-in to exclude Authenticator from battery optimization. No configuration action.
items.why: Help desks will see users asking about restore banners and a rating prompt that appears during sign-in; a user who has learned that Authenticator shows unexpected prompts is easier to talk into approving the wrong one.
items.action: Tell the service desk and update end-user screenshots; remind users that the rating prompt never asks for a number or an approval.

items.title: MSRC discloses CVE-2026-97785, an elevation of privilege in Entra Application Proxy rated 10.0; Microsoft has fully mitigated it and customers have nothing to do
items.officialTitle: CVE-2026-97785 AAD App Proxy Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
items.fingerprint: Released 22 October 2026, CVSS 10.0, Critical, not exploited and not publicly disclosed: improper authentication in AAD App Proxy allowed an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network. The FAQ says the vulnerability has already been fully mitigated by Microsoft and there is no action for users of the service.
items.why: Application Proxy publishes on-premises apps to the internet under Entra pre-authentication; a 10.0 authentication flaw there is worth recording against any unexplained App Proxy access before the mitigation date, which Microsoft does not state.
items.action: No patch. If you publish apps through Application Proxy, note the CVE in the risk register and check App Proxy sign-in and connector logs for anomalies you could not explain earlier.

items.title: MSRC publishes five more already-mitigated cloud CVEs: Azure Kubernetes Configuration Service and VM Inspector (10.0), Azure Pipelines (9.1), Azure AI Foundry (7.7), Exchange Online (7.5)
items.fingerprint: Released 22 October 2026, all Critical, none exploited or publicly disclosed, each with Microsoft's FAQ stating the vulnerability has been fully mitigated and there is no customer action: CVE-2026-83938 Azure Kubernetes Configuration Service EoP (10.0, missing authentication), CVE-2026-110063 VM Inspector for Azure Virtual Machines EoP (10.0, link following), CVE-2026-105014 Azure Pipelines RCE (9.1, command injection), CVE-2026-108456 Azure AI Foundry EoP (7.7, SSRF), CVE-2026-96185 Exchange Online RCE (7.5, stack-based buffer overflow).
items.why: Cloud-service CVEs carry no patch, so they reach a SOC only as a disclosure; they are the record to cite if an investigation later finds activity on one of these services before the mitigation.
items.action: No action. Record the five CVEs against the services you use; nothing to deploy.

items.title: App management policies gain an audit state in Graph beta: evaluate credential and app restrictions without enforcing them
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Graph what's new — October 2026: New in preview only — Applications
items.tier0Note: App management policies restrict how secrets and certificates are added to applications and service principals, the persistence path used against app-only identities.
items.fingerprint: Graph's what's new for October 2026 (commit 7c8942a 'Document public audit state', 21 October) adds the audit member to the appManagementRestrictionState enumeration used by appManagementPolicy, to evaluate application management policy restrictions without enforcing them.
items.why: An audit mode is how a tenant can measure what a 'no client secrets' or 'max credential lifetime' policy would break before switching it on, which is the usual reason those policies are never enforced.
items.action: Where app management policies are still off, plan an audit-state rollout of the credential restrictions and review what it reports; the value is beta-only.

items.title: Auto-expanding archive mailboxes can grow to 3 TB instead of 1.5 TB for eligible licences (GCC, GCC High and DoD, mid-November to early December)
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Purview: Data Lifecycle Management increases the auto-expanding archive limit from 1.5 TB to 3 TB
items.fingerprint: General availability for GCC, GCC High and DoD rolls out from mid-November 2026 to early December 2026: the maximum auto-expanding archive rises from 1.5 TB to 3 TB for mailboxes with eligible licences (E5, A5, G5, several Purview Suite and F5 Compliance SKUs); others stay at 1.5 TB; no per-GB charge and no change to retention, policies or holds; no configuration required.
items.why: Larger archives mean larger eDiscovery and content-search scopes during an investigation; storage is not a security control but it changes how long a search over a held mailbox takes.
items.action: Awareness only; update eDiscovery runbooks that assume a 1.5 TB ceiling.

items.title: Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 adds a Move to Quarantine remediation action: admins can pull suspicious mail from mailboxes into Defender quarantine, rollout early November to mid-December 2026
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Defender for Office 365: Move email messages to quarantine with a new remediation action
items.fingerprint: Published 23 October 2026. A new Move to Quarantine action in the Take Action wizard (Defender for Office 365 Plan 2) moves selected messages from Inbox, Junk Email, Deleted Items and recoverable items into Defender quarantine under a quarantine policy the admin picks (admin-only by default), with the reason Admin triggered; the action shows in the Unified Action Center, Threat Explorer, Advanced Hunting, custom detections and the email entity page. GA rollout starts early November and completes by mid-December 2026; approving it needs the Search and Purge role.
items.why: It is a reversible containment option between Move to Junk and Soft/Hard delete: the evidence stays reviewable and releasable, and the action is audited in the Action Center, so phishing response no longer has to choose between leaving mail in reach of the user and destroying it.
items.action: Before November decide which quarantine policy the action should use, confirm who holds Search and Purge, and add Move to Quarantine to the phishing and BEC playbooks as the default containment step.

items.title: Defender's new Threat intelligence experience: Overview and Intel explorer replace the Threat analytics and Intel management pages; Threat analytics types are renamed (Actor to Threat actor, Activity to Campaign, Technique to Attack patterns)
items.officialTitle: Turn threat intelligence into informed action with Microsoft Defender
items.reference: no MC/RM post — Microsoft Defender XDR Blog
items.fingerprint: Published 22 October 2026. Threat intelligence in the Defender portal is reorganised into Overview (latest, high-impact and highest-exposure threats, executive summary from the Threat Intelligence Briefing Agent) and Intel explorer (keyword search and filters across Microsoft, connected third-party and your own intelligence); the blog says they replace Threat Analytics and Intel Management, Microsoft's transition article maps the old Threat Analytics types to new names and moves the Relationships tab into entity details.

items.action: Update the TI runbook and analyst bookmarks to Threat intelligence > Overview and Intel explorer, and re-check any email notification and custom-detection links that pointed at Threat analytics reports.

items.title: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys compromised: Windows blocked the CAs on 20 October, an out-of-band update removes seven eMudhra roots on 26 October and Edge follows on 27 October
items.officialTitle: New MSRC blog: Microsoft’s response to compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys
items.tier0Note: Certificate trust is tier 0: a certificate chaining to a compromised CA can impersonate TLS endpoints and sign code that Windows treats as trusted.
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft states the Edge trust-list removal on 27 October 2026; the Windows out-of-band update is available from 26 October.
items.fingerprint: MSRC (26 October 2026): eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys (six TLS, two code signing) were compromised in eMudhra's hierarchy, not at Microsoft. 20 October: the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List blocks the affected CAs; Edge and WebView2 block the TLS certificates through CRLSet. 26 October: out-of-band Windows updates (KB5134133 for Windows 11 24H2/25H2/26H2, KB5134137 for Server 2025, KB5134140 for Server 2022, KB5134123-25 and KB5134130/34 for the rest) remove six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign. 27 October: the same seven leave the Edge trust list.
items.why: A certificate that chains to a compromised CA can impersonate a TLS endpoint or sign code that Windows trusts; disconnected or WSUS-only devices that never received the 20 October Disallowed list still trust it.
items.action: Make sure the Disallowed CTL and the 26 October out-of-band update reach devices without automatic root updates (offline, WSUS-only, Azure images); inventory certificates chaining to the seven removed roots and replace them before they stop validating.

items.title: Advanced hunting gains a MessageContents table with Teams message snippets; GA now completes by mid-November, not mid-October
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Microsoft Defender for Office 365: New MessageContents table in Advanced Hunting for Microsoft Teams messages
items.fingerprint: Revised 26 October 2026: GA rollout began late September and now completes by mid-November 2026 (previously mid-October). The MessageContents table exposes Teams message snippets and metadata, including messages with URLs and federated messages, to analysts holding the Advanced Hunting and message preview permissions.
items.why: A hunting table that holds Teams message content is a new place where message text is readable; who holds message preview permission decides who can read it.
items.action: Decide which analysts hold the Advanced Hunting and message preview permissions before the table reaches your tenant, and add MessageContents to your Teams phishing hunting once it appears.

items.title: Teams starts decoding QR codes in chats and channels and warns on malicious destinations from early November, internal senders included
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Teams: Malicious QR code detection in messages
items.fingerprint: GA begins early November and completes mid-November 2026. Teams decodes QR codes in inline images in 1:1, group and meeting chats and channels, internal and external, and shows 'This message contains a link that might be harmful' when the destination is malicious. Governed by the existing Malicious URL protection setting (on by default); no separate control.
items.why: QR-code phishing in Teams has had no URL verdict until now; the warning gives users and the help desk a signal, and internal senders, whose QR images are not blurred, are covered too.
items.action: Check Teams admin center > Messaging Safety has Malicious URL protection on, and brief the help desk on the new warning and on blurring being a separate, non-verdict experience.

items.title: Teams blurs QR-code images from external senders by default; GA moves to late October
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Microsoft Teams: QR code protection for messages from external users
items.fingerprint: Revised 26 October 2026: Targeted Release begins and completes mid-October (previously early October); General Availability begins and completes late October 2026 (previously mid-October). Images with QR codes from external senders are blurred by default; users can reveal them; blurring is not a malicious verdict. No admin control.
items.why: External QR images reach users blurred from this week, which changes what a phishing report from a Teams chat looks like.
items.action: Tell users and the help desk that blurred QR images from external senders are expected and are not a malicious verdict.

items.title: Exchange Online Change Optics report is GA: it lists onmicrosoft.com external traffic and Direct Send traffic before enforcement
items.officialTitle: Change Optics Report
items.fingerprint: GA worldwide on 26 October 2026 (preview was MC1301802). EAC > Reports > Mail flow > Change Optics Report shows sample messages for two scenarios: OMC (onmicrosoft.com traffic sent externally, affected by onmicrosoft.com throttling) and DRS (Direct Send traffic received by the tenant, to find legitimate senders before enabling Reject Direct Send).
items.why: Direct Send is a spoofing path that Reject Direct Send closes; the report is the inventory of legitimate senders you need before you switch it on.
items.action: Open the DRS scenario in the Change Optics report, list the legitimate Direct Send senders, move them to a connector or authenticated submission, then enable Reject Direct Send.

items.title: Conditional Access policy plans (preview) are now documented: shared targeting and exclusions defined once, inherited by every rule, and a plan-level exclusion no rule can remove
items.officialTitle: What are Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policy plans? (preview)
items.tier0Note: Conditional Access is the tenant's access-control plane: a plan's shared conditions decide targeting and emergency-access exclusions for every rule it holds.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft added three pages on 26 October 2026 (entra-docs b575484, ms.date 21 October): a plan groups rules under shared assignments and conditions (identities, applications, user actions, authentication context, risk, platforms, locations, client apps). Plan-level targeting is inherited and cannot be narrowed by a rule; plan and rule exclusions accumulate and a plan exclusion can never be removed by a rule; each rule is evaluated as an independent policy and appears separately in sign-in logs. During preview, plans that target users with a location condition get one-hour tokens without the instant IP enforcement check. Creating, changing or deleting a plan needs Conditional Access Administrator.
items.why: Sign-in logs will show plan rules as separate entries, and a plan-level exclusion silently applies to every rule; location-conditioned plans lose continuous access evaluation's instant IP enforcement during preview.
items.action: Before adopting plans, decide where emergency-access exclusions live, make sure sign-in log parsing and CA reporting handle rule entries, and keep location-based policies outside plans while the one-hour-token limitation applies.

items.title: Six CopilotCostManagement permissions appear in Microsoft's 27 October permission sync, covering Copilot spending policies and per-user usage reports
items.officialTitle: Weekly Permissions sync 2026-10-27 (permissions-update/2026-10-27, not merged to master)
items.reference: no MC/RM post — permission file only
items.fingerprint: Commit 41979b0 (27 October 2026, branch permissions-update/2026-10-27, not merged to master) adds CopilotCostManagement.Read.All, CopilotCostManagement-Assignment.Read.All, CopilotCostManagement-Assignment.ReadWrite.All, CopilotCostManagement-Policy.Read.All, CopilotCostManagement-Policy.ReadWrite.All and CopilotCostManagement-UserData.Read.All, mapped to /copilot/costManagement/spendingPolicies, its assignedGroups and emailThresholdSettings, getTenantCreditBalance and the usageReports (user, group, service and funding usage records).
items.why: CopilotCostManagement-UserData.Read.All reads per-user Copilot usage details and sessions; the ReadWrite permissions let an app change spending policies and which groups they apply to. Neither is in Microsoft's permissions reference yet.
items.action: No tenant action until the permissions reach the service; once they do, add the CopilotCostManagement.* names to the consent watch list and alert on any grant of the ReadWrite or UserData permissions.

roles: Microsoft Entra Joined Device Local Administrator

graphMap.rule: resource = first path segment that is not a parameter; /me/... counts as users. Directory action microsoft.directory/<resource>[/<property>]/<operation>; a .unified or .security suffix on the resource falls back to its base. GET maps to read, POST to create, PATCH and PUT to update, DELETE to delete. A role covers an endpoint when it holds an action on the same resource with the same operation, or allTasks on that resource. Coverage is the share of the permission's ENDPOINTS, never the count of the role's actions. Depth is whole resource when the matching action carries allProperties or allTasks, and selected properties only otherwise.
graphMap.ruleNote: Derived by this brief, not published by Microsoft. Microsoft publishes no role-to-permission mapping: permissions.json carries authorizationType, ownerInfo, pathSets and schemes and no role field at all, and the 136 role source files in MicrosoftDocs/entra-docs name no Graph permission.
